overview.description: Fipsen is a unique northern German trick-taking game, traditionally played in the coastal regions between Hamburg and Bremen. It belongs to the 'One vs. All' family of games, similar to Nap or Skat. Fipsen is distinguished by its highly specialized 25-card deckâ€”where the 7 of Diamonds (the 'Rute') is the only card of its suit allowedâ€”and its aggressive doubling mechanics. The game is a test of risk management, where players bid on the number of tricks they can win using a limited hand of just five cards.

history.origins: Fipsen originated in the 19th century as a favorite game among farmers and sailors in Northern Germany. While its popularity has waned since the midnd20th century, it remains a cultural centerpiece in the town of Prisdorf, where Fipsen tournaments are held alongside Skat events.
timeline: 1800s: Fipsen emerges as a popular rural gambling game in SchleswigndHolstein.
1900s: Regional variations like 'Karo Fipsen' and 'Thedinghausen Fipsen' develop.
2009: Documented internationally after being highlighted on German social cruises.
Present: Actively preserved by local clubs north of Hamburg.
history.evolution: The game's deck strippingâ€”removing almost all Diamondsâ€”is a unique evolutionary quirk that emphasizes suit concentration and makes 'Ruten' (Diamonds) bids extremely highndrisk.
history.cultural: In northern Germany, Fipsen is often associated with communal gatherings and is played with a distinct local dialect (Low German).

setup.players: 4 players (standard). Each player plays for themselves, but three act as a temporary team against the highest bidder.
setup.deck: 25 cards. Start with a 32ndcard Skat deck and remove all Diamonds except the Seven of Diamonds.
setup.dealing: Each player receives 5 cards (traditionally 3 then 2). Two cards are dealt face-down to the center (the Skat). Three cards are left over and set aside.

rules.objective: Win the number of tricks declared during the bidding phase. If the bidder succeeds, they win points; if they fail, they are penalized.
rules.gameplay:
1. Lead: The bidder leads the first trick.
2. Following Suit: Players must follow suit if possible.
3. Trumps: If you cannot follow suit, you may play a trump.
keyRules: Siebener Fips: If a player is dealt all four Sevens (Club, Spade, Heart, and Diamond) plus an Ace, they win immediately and score 30 points.
Doubling: Scoring values double if Clubs are trumps or if a player declares 'Diamonds' (Ruten).
Kloppen: An opponent can 'Knock' (Kloppen) to double the stakes again.

strategy.basic: In Fipsen, with only 5 cards, an Ace-heavy hand is nearly unbeatable. If you hold two Aces, bid at least 3 tricks.
strategy.intermediate: The 'Ruten' Trap: Be very careful bidding Diamonds. Since there is only ONE trump (the 7 of Diamonds), once it is played, the game reverts to plain suits. Only bid Ruten if you have strong length in a nonndtrump suit.
strategy.advanced: Defensive Coordination: The three defenders must work together to bleed the bidder's trumps. If the bidder leads an Ace, the defenders should throw their highest offndsuit cards to force a trump play later.
tips: The 'Kieker' bid is powerful but dangerousâ€”use it only if your initial 5 cards are all different suits and low values.
Track the Sevens! Every Seven played reduces the chance of someone hitting a 'Siebener Fips'.

variations.noVariationsReason: Only the standard Prisdorf form is encoded; regional variants (Großenaspe, Thedinghausen, Mecklenburg) are documented in sources but not listed as separate variations.

difficulty.easy: Fails to utilize the Skat correctly; bids 2 tricks with weak hands; doesn't recognize the power of the 7 of Diamonds.
difficulty.medium: Bids based on Ace-count; understands Doubling for Clubs and Ruten; plays defensively with partners.
difficulty.hard: Perfectly calculates the probability of the missing 7 of Diamonds being in the Skat; uses 'Kieker' to completely reconstruct a losing hand; uses 'Kloppen' to force folds.

considerations: AI must handle the '1 vs 3' team dynamic and understand that defenders should not compete against each other.

additional: The Playing Card Vol 49, No 1 (2020) - Paul Eaton

engine.deckDescription: One full deck of 52 cards using French suits (hearts, diamonds, clubs, spades) and standard ranks from ace through king, with no jokers.
engine.suitDescription: French suits: hearts (cœurs), diamonds (carreaux), clubs (trèfles), and spades (piques). Each suit has thirteen cards from ace through king.
engine.rankDescription: Standard ranking for a 52-card deck: ace (high or low by context), king, queen, jack, 10, 9, 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2. Thirteen cards per suit.

hero.title: FIPSEN
hero.subtitle: The German Solo Trick-Taker
hero.tagline: Bid, play, and try to make your tricksâ€”or lose to three defenders.

synthesis.shortDescription: A German solo bidding trick-taking game where one player bids to make a certain number of tricks against three defenders.

prompts.human: Welcome to Fipsen! Bid for the number of tricks you think you can make (1-8). If you win the bidding, you play solo against the other three players. Make your bid and you score the bid amount; fail and you lose those points. The 7 of Diamonds is specialâ€”watch for it!
prompts.ai: Game: Fipsen (German solo trick-taker). 3-5 players (optimal 4). 32-card deck (some regions use 36). Bidding: Each player bids 1-8 tricks (highest bidder becomes soloist). Soloist may draw from Skat (optional). Gameplay: 8 tricks total. Lead player starts; others follow suit if able. Scoring: Soloist scores bid amount if they make bid tricks; lose bid amount if fail. Defenders win if soloist fails. Rotate bidder for next round.

scoring.description: Trick-based scoring. Bidder tries to achieve bid tricks; defenders try to stop them. Points awarded based on bid success.
scoring.winCondition: Bidder wins if tricks taken >= bid. Defenders win if bidder fails. Game continues with rotating bidder.
scoring.splitRules: Solo bidder vs 3 defenders. No pot splitting.

nullReasons.targetScore: Game does not use target score.
nullReasons.scoringDirection: Game does not use scoring direction.
nullReasons.cardValues: Scoring is based on making or failing the bid; no per-card point values.
